card_headline: Taiwan goes to local elections on 28 November with a split government, AI-driven record growth, a stalled $14 billion US arms package and Chinese coast guard pressure
card_summary: Taiwan votes in nine-in-one local elections on 28 November under a divided government: Lai's DPP holds the executive, the KMT and TPP the legislature. [1] The legislature capped a special defence budget at US$24.8 billion. [2] Beijing calls Taiwan its internal affair, Taipei says the Republic of China is sovereign, and Washington takes no position. [3] A $14 billion US arms package is stalled. [4] DGBAS forecasts 11.05 percent growth for 2026. [5]
card_local: Taipei Times and Focus Taiwan (CNA, which is state-funded) report conflicting polls in the Taichung mayoral race and an allegation by prosecutors that a small-party leader ran with CCP direction. [1][6]
card_international: AP reports that Taiwan is likely to take a backseat at the Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen and that the $14 billion arms package is stalled; Xinhua says Trump told Xi the US does not support Taiwan independence, which Washington has not confirmed. [4][7]
card_scholar: CFR's David Sacks says Beijing wants the arms sale delayed, possibly into 2027, and the US-China Commission says PLA air activity is lower in 2026 while coast guard and fleet pressure is at a record. [8][9]
context_md: Taiwan has been governed separately from the People's Republic of China since 1949, and Beijing claims it. [10] The Taipei government says the Republic of China is a sovereign state, Beijing calls Taiwan purely its internal affair, and the United States says it takes no position on sovereignty. [3][11] President Lai Ching-te of the DPP holds the executive, while the KMT and TPP control the legislature, which can cut or freeze defence funds but cannot add line items. [12] Taiwan produces more than 90 percent of the world's advanced semiconductors, and TSMC holds 72 percent of global foundry revenue. [9] Freedom House scored Taiwan 93 out of 100 in 2026 and rated it Free. [13] The island holds nine-in-one local elections on 28 November 2026, ahead of the January 2028 national elections. [14]

sections.title: Who says what about Taiwan's status: three positions and a shrinking middle
sections.body_md:
This page reports positions and does not rule on them. The Taiwan government says the Republic of China is a sovereign state, that Beijing has never ruled Taiwan, and that UN Resolution 2758 does not mention Taiwan. President Lai has said the two sides are "not subordinate to each other". [3] The Mainland Affairs Council, Taipei's China policy body, said in April that describing the strait as a "one family" matter misstates a sovereignty dispute as an internal one. [15]

Beijing's Taiwan Affairs Office calls the question "purely China's internal affair" and tells Washington to stop arms sales. [11] Spokesperson Chen Binhua said in January that Lai's agenda will bring war and that "reunification is the only viable path". [16] Both outlets are PRC state media. The PRC also argues that Resolution 2758 settles Taiwan's status, a reading the US State Department has rejected, according to Malay Mail. [3]

Washington takes no position on sovereignty, severed official ties in 1979 and is legally bound to help Taiwan defend itself. Only 12 countries recognise Taipei. [3] Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on 19 November that Tokyo's Taiwan policy is unchanged and consistent with the 1972 Japan-China communique, after her November 2025 remarks that a blockade could threaten Japan's survival. [17]

Public opinion is measured differently by different pollsters. A National Development Foundation poll in June found 58.0 percent rejecting the one China principle as a precondition for talks and 25.8 percent accepting it. [18] The US-China Commission reports that 4 percent of Taiwanese support unification, though 30 percent expect it to happen. [9]

lenses.local: Focus Taiwan (CNA) reports the Mainland Affairs Council's deputy head saying Taiwan is unlikely to be the focus of the Shenzhen talks; Taiwan's APEC envoy is Stan Shih, appointed by Lai. [19]
lenses.international: Global Times, a PRC state outlet, relays Xinhua's account that Trump said the US does not support Taiwan independence. [20] IBTimes UK notes there is no US confirmation of that remark. [7]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group's 2023 report found that the political understandings that kept the peace were weakening, and recommended both credible deterrence and mutual assurances. [21]

sections.title: Pressure has shifted from large drills to the coast guard and area denial
sections.body_md:
China's Eastern Theatre Command held a 10-hour live-fire exercise called Justice Mission 2025 on 30 December 2025. Taiwan's defence ministry counted 71 Chinese military aircraft and 24 navy and coast guard vessels, and Reuters called it the sixth major round of war games since 2022. [22] The drills followed a record US arms package of $11.1 billion, and Beijing had warned it would take forceful measures. [22]

The air tempo then fell. The Taiwan Security Monitor at George Mason University counted 190 PLA aircraft sorties in February 2026, down from 270 in January and 492 in February 2025, with ten China Coast Guard incursions into restricted waters in January and February, eight near Kinmen. [23] The US-China Commission describes ADIZ entries as almost daily but lower in 2026 than in Lai's first two years. [9]

The coast guard line moved east. On 8 June Taiwan's coast guard said it had expelled four Chinese ships, and Xinhua described a transport ministry operation east of Taiwan as a response to Japan and the Philippines opening boundary talks. [24] Al Jazeera reported 55 sightings of Chinese coast guard and research vessels in June against 30 in May. Ray Powell of Stanford's Sea Light said the patrols could mark the start of a quarantine, while China's foreign ministry calls them lawful exercises of jurisdiction. [25]

In November, defence minister Wellington Koo confirmed area denial drills involving the Liaoning carrier group, and National Security Council chief Joseph Wu reported more than 100 Chinese naval and coast guard ships nearby. [26] Analyst Su Tzu-yun called one early November day of 49 aircraft a "quiet exercise" without a formal drill announcement. [27] On National Day, 21 aircraft and seven ships were logged, and Lai said defence spending aims to deter war, not provoke it. [10]

lenses.local: Taipei Times reports Taiwan's defence minister and security chief describing area denial drills and 100-plus ships, and CommonWealth Magazine has published a data graphic on Chinese coast guard signals around Taiwan, which could not be opened for this draft. [26][28]
lenses.international: AFP and Reuters carry the Taiwan coast guard's account and Xinhua's account side by side, and Al Jazeera adds that the UK, Germany and France opposed any unilateral change to the status quo. [24][25]
lenses.scholar: The Taiwan Security Monitor and the US-China Commission both record lower air tempo in 2026 alongside record maritime pressure. [23][9]

sections.title: Washington: a stalled $14 billion package and a Xinhua readout nobody has confirmed
sections.body_md:
The Trump administration authorised a record $11 billion package in December 2025, and lawmakers approved a separate $14 billion sale in January that cannot advance until Trump formally sends it to Congress. [29] After the May summit in Beijing, Trump said he had not decided whether to advance a major package and would make a determination. Chinese officials said Xi warned that mishandling Taiwan could lead to "clashes and even conflicts". [29]

By late September the $14 billion package was still stalled. Taiwan's defence minister, Wellington Koo, said Taipei had received no notice of changes and that US officials assured him policy had not changed. [30] CFR's David Sacks wrote that Xi pressed Washington to keep opposing Taiwan independence, that Taiwan was absent from both sides' readouts, and that Beijing may want the sale stalled into 2027. [8]

On 19 November, after the Shenzhen meeting, Xinhua said Xi told Trump to do the right thing on Taiwan and that Trump said the US does not support Taiwan independence. [19] IBTimes UK reports no US confirmation and no Taiwanese government response. [7]

Delays in deliveries are explained differently. AP quotes Kuo Yu-jen of the Institute for National Policy Research saying missile deliveries are slow because production capacity is limited, not for political reasons. Taiwan's backlog of US orders totals almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor as cited by AP. [4]

lenses.local: Taiwan's defence minister says Taipei has received no notice of US policy changes, and the Mainland Affairs Council's deputy head says Taiwan is unlikely to be the focus at Shenzhen. [30][19]
lenses.international: AP reports that few expect breakthroughs on Taiwan at the Shenzhen meeting and that US-Taiwan cooperation continues behind the scenes. [4]
lenses.scholar: CFR's Sacks calls the September summit high on symbolism and low on substance, and says a long delay in the arms sale could erode Taiwan's confidence in US reliability. [8]

sections.title: The chip economy: 11 percent growth, a tariff deal in limbo and a single point of failure
sections.body_md:
Taiwan's statistics agency, DGBAS, raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11.05 percent in August, the fastest since 1987, with merchandise exports forecast at US$903.6 billion, up 41.19 percent. [5] ICT goods made up 44 percent of exports from January to September, against 14 percent in 2021, and unemployment was 3.4 percent in August, according to East Asia Forum author Min-Hua Chiang. She also notes household debt above 90 percent of GDP. [31]

TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1 billion, with revenue up 51 percent and high-performance computing at 68 percent of sales. Its second Arizona fab has finished construction, with mass production due in the third quarter of 2027, and chief executive C.C. Wei said the company is prudent about 2027. [32]

The US tariff position is unsettled. In January 2026 the two governments agreed a 15 percent US tariff on Taiwan, down from 32 percent, and Taiwan pledged $250 billion of semiconductor investment plus $250 billion in credit guarantees. The Supreme Court then ruled against the emergency-powers basis for the 2025 tariffs, and the president imposed a 10 percent global tariff for 150 days. CRS said the deal may be hard to pass in Taiwan's opposition-controlled legislature. [33] East Asia Forum puts the rate Taiwan faces at 10 percent. [31] The current rate was not confirmed for this draft.

Concentration is the risk. The US-China Commission says Taiwan makes over 90 percent of advanced chips, and Chatham House cites a Bloomberg forecast that a Chinese blockade would cut global GDP by about 5 percent. [9][34]

lenses.local: Focus Taiwan (CNA) reports the government's own forecast of 11.05 percent growth for 2026 and 6.04 percent for 2027. [5]
lenses.international: The Next Web, summarising TSMC's results, reports demand still exceeds capacity even as consumer markets come under pressure. [32]
lenses.scholar: East Asia Forum's Min-Hua Chiang warns that reduced AI-chip purchases by large US firms could hurt the economy, and Chatham House argues a Taiwan crisis would do more global damage than a Hormuz closure. [31][34]

sections.title: A divided government, a capped defence budget and a 28 November test
sections.body_md:
All 24 KMT legislators up for recall survived the vote on 26 July 2025, which CFR's David Sacks said would likely embolden the KMT to oppose Lai's agenda. [35] Lai then proposed a $40 billion special defence budget for 2026 to 2033, aiming for 5 percent of GDP by 2030, and the KMT and TPP blocked its first review. [36] The KMT offered about $12 billion focused on US systems. [12] On 8 May the legislature passed a bill with a ceiling of NT$780 billion, about US$24.8 billion. [2] The US-China Commission says that is roughly 60 percent of the goal, with most domestic asymmetric programmes cut. [9] Gahon Chiang, a staff member of a DPP legislator, argues the act's stage limits could block urgent purchases. [37]

An impeachment motion against Lai failed on 19 May. [38] On 10 April KMT chair Cheng Li-wun met Xi in Beijing, where both opposed Taiwan independence and Cheng spoke of reconciliation. Lai said compromise with authoritarian regimes "only sacrifices sovereignty and democracy". [15]

The 28 November elections choose local leaders, but Courtney Donovan Smith writes that they will shape the players for January 2028, and that Lai may resign as DPP chair if the party does badly. [14] In Taichung, five polls conflict: four put KMT's Johnny Chiang ahead, while one on 3 November had DPP's Ho Hsin-chun ahead 41.1 to 30.4. [1] In Kaohsiung, KMT's Ko Chih-en faces DPP's Lai Jui-lung. [39] In Taipei, incumbent KMT mayor Chiang Wan-an faces DPP's Puma Shen. [40]

lenses.local: Focus Taiwan (CNA) and Taipei Times cover the campaign race by race, and Taipei Times carries both a DPP staffer's critique of the budget act and a columnist's forecast of the vote. [1][37][14]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports that Cheng's Beijing trip was viewed with scepticism, particularly among DPP supporters. [15]
lenses.scholar: Brookings' Drew Thompson expected a compromise on the budget, smaller than Lai's proposal, given broad public support for defence spending. [12]

sections.title: Interference claims and a free but polarised press
sections.body_md:
Taiwan's National Security Bureau warned in April that China may interfere in the November elections. It reported more than 173 million attacks on the government network in the first quarter and about 13,000 suspicious accounts spreading 860,000 disputed messages, some AI-generated. [41] Beijing has repeatedly denied interfering in Taiwan's elections and accuses the DPP of promoting separatism, according to RFA. [42]

On 9 November, prosecutors in Tainan and Hsinchu questioned defendants in a case in which they allege Lin Te-wang, leader of the Taiwan People's Communist Party, stood for office with CCP direction and funding and sent voters to China for free services. A court held him incommunicado, and the Taiwan Affairs Office had not commented. This rests on one outlet and the allegations are untested. [6]

Freedom House gave Taiwan 93 out of 100, one point down, citing polarisation, weak protection for migrant workers, Chinese influence efforts and a Constitutional Court that lacked a quorum for most of the year. [13] RSF ranked Taiwan 28th, down four places, and attributed the fall to polarisation and falling public trust. [43] The Reuters Institute finds that 25 percent of Taiwanese trust news, and that TVBS reportedly faces its first loss and has cut about 45 news roles. [44]

The Reporter, a nonprofit outlet founded in 2015 and funded by reader donations, is one of the independent investigative voices in this market. [45]

lenses.local: Taipei Times via Liberty Times carries the security bureau's election warnings, and The Reporter says it relies on reader donations rather than commercial advertising. [41][45]
lenses.international: RFA reports analysts expect AI deepfakes and impersonation before 28 November, and that attributing online activity to China is difficult. [42]
lenses.scholar: The Reuters Institute reports low trust in news and a weak advertising market, and Freedom House cites polarisation and Chinese influence efforts. [44][13]

US and Taiwan agree a 15 percent US tariff and $250 billion of Taiwan chip investment.
US Supreme Court rules against the emergency-powers basis for the 2025 tariffs.
KMT chair Cheng Li-wun meets Xi Jinping in Beijing.
The legislature passes a special arms budget capped at NT$780 billion.

Taiwan expels four Chinese ships as Beijing announces a maritime enforcement operation east of Taiwan.

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: Liberty Times (LTN) was reached only through its Taipei Times English pages, and the Chinese-language pages of Liberty Times, The Reporter and CommonWealth were not read. The CommonWealth data graphic could not be opened.
Focus Taiwan (CNA) and TaiwanPlus are publicly funded; their reports are used for facts and not flagged state_affiliated, but readers should know the funding.

PRC state media were read only through Global Times and People's Daily Online; Xinhua and the Taiwan Affairs Office pages were not opened directly, and the Chinese foreign ministry readout of the 19 November meeting could not be fetched.
No US readout of the Xi-Trump meeting in Shenzhen was found, so the Xinhua claim is unconfirmed.
The current US tariff rate on Taiwan is unclear: CRS (March) and East Asia Forum (October) give different figures and the legal basis changed in February.
Several Taipei Times and Focus Taiwan items had no headline, byline or full text in the page text; vote counts for the budget and impeachment votes were not retrieved.
Taiwan government figures (defence ministry, NSB, DGBAS) are taken as reported by outlets and were not checked against primary releases.
Polling on unification and identity is from one poll (NDF) and one commission summary; no recent NCCU Election Study Center figures were retrieved.
Only one podcast and no verified documentary or photo essay were found, so the podcast and media lists are short.
The ACLED, UCDP or UN conflict-data lens does not apply to Taiwan, and no humanitarian data were sought; scores reflect gray-zone and political risk.
Severity scores are low for violence and humanitarian parts because there is no armed conflict; the case for concern rests on the gi block, which is contingency-based.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters, AFP and Al Jazeera file on Taiwan regularly, and think tanks such as CFR, Brookings, Chatham House and the US-China Commission publish steadily [4][22][24][25]. Coverage spikes around drills, summits and arms decisions, while domestic politics and the press market get less English-language attention [9][44].

severity.basis: There is no armed conflict, but Taiwan logged a 71-aircraft live-fire encirclement in December 2025 and more than 100 Chinese ships around the island in November 2026 [22][26].
No displacement or hunger crisis is reported in the sources reviewed, and Taiwan's unemployment rate was 3.4 percent in August [31].
Freedom House rates Taiwan Free at 93 out of 100 while citing polarisation and a Constitutional Court that lacked a quorum for most of the year [13].
GDP is forecast to grow 11.05 percent in 2026, though household debt exceeds 90 percent of GDP and exports depend on AI chips [5][31].
PLA air activity fell in 2026, but coast guard patrols east of Taiwan and area denial drills grew and arms deliveries are delayed [23][25][26].

parts.basis: The US is Taiwan's largest informal ally and arms supplier, China claims it, and Japan's prime minister has linked a Taiwan blockade to Japan's own security [4][17].
Taiwan makes over 90 percent of advanced chips and TSMC holds 72 percent of foundry revenue, and Chatham House cites a 5 percent global GDP loss from a blockade [9][34].
A Taiwan crisis could draw in the US, Japan and the Philippines, as the June boundary-talks dispute and the area denial drills show [24][26].
A war or blockade would hit global supply chains and economies far beyond the island, and Chatham House puts a blockade at about 5 percent of global GDP [34].
The status dispute touches UN Resolution 2758 and the US Six Assurances, which Taipei, Beijing and Washington read differently [3][29].

summary: Taiwan scores high on global implications because chips, great-power commitments and a contested legal status meet in one place [9][3][4]. Its direct humanitarian and diaspora reach is small beside that.
The score rests on contingencies, not on events inside Taiwan today. A blockade or quarantine would be priced in trade and in alliance commitments well beyond the strait [34].
gi.up: A Chinese quarantine or blockade, a formal US shift on arms sales, or a breakdown of the TSMC supply chain.
gi.down: A durable US-China arrangement with deliveries resuming, or diversification of advanced chip production beyond Taiwan.

international_md:
Global Times, a PRC state outlet, relays Xinhua's account that Trump said the US does not support Taiwan independence. [20] IBTimes UK notes there is no US confirmation of that remark. [7]

AFP and Reuters carry the Taiwan coast guard's account and Xinhua's account side by side, and Al Jazeera adds that the UK, Germany and France opposed any unilateral change to the status quo. [24][25]

scholar_md:
Crisis Group's 2023 report found that the political understandings that kept the peace were weakening, and recommended both credible deterrence and mutual assurances. [21]

The Taiwan Security Monitor and the US-China Commission both record lower air tempo in 2026 alongside record maritime pressure. [23][9]

CFR's Sacks calls the September summit high on symbolism and low on substance, and says a long delay in the arms sale could erode Taiwan's confidence in US reliability. [8]

East Asia Forum's Min-Hua Chiang warns that reduced AI-chip purchases by large US firms could hurt the economy, and Chatham House argues a Taiwan crisis would do more global damage than a Hormuz closure. [31][34]

Brookings' Drew Thompson expected a compromise on the budget, smaller than Lai's proposal, given broad public support for defence spending. [12]

The Reuters Institute reports low trust in news and a weak advertising market, and Freedom House cites polarisation and Chinese influence efforts. [44][13]
